sections.heading: A separate account of Athena’s birth
sections.translation:
Hera raged and quarreled with her husband.
Out of this quarrel she bore a glorious son,
Hephaestus, without making love with Zeus, who carries the aegis.
His handiwork surpassed that of all the heavenly gods.
But Zeus, away from Hera, lay with the lovely-cheeked daughter
of Oceanus and Tethys with her beautiful hair.

[Gap in the Greek source]

He deceived Metis, though she knew so many tricks.
He seized her in his hands and put her inside his belly,
afraid she might bear another child stronger than his thunderbolt.
That was why Zeus, son of Cronus, enthroned on high,
living in the upper air, suddenly swallowed her.
At once she conceived Pallas Athena.
Then the father of gods and humans gave birth to Athena
from his head, beside the banks of the river Triton.

Metis, Athena’s mother, stayed hidden
beneath the organs inside Zeus’s body.
She shaped what was right and knew more
than all the gods and mortal humans.
There the goddess had found a place; from there,
her handiwork surpassed that of all the immortals
who have their homes on Olympus.
[She made the aegis, Athena’s armor that sends armies fleeing.]
With it, Zeus brought Athena to birth, wearing her battle gear.
sections.summary: In this separate version, Hera bears Hephaestus without Zeus. Zeus swallows Metis, who conceives Athena inside him. Athena is born from his head, equipped for battle.

cards.label: Hera
cards.here: After quarreling with Zeus, she bears Hephaestus without him.

cards.label: Hephaestus
cards.general: The god of metalworking and skilled craftsmanship.
cards.here: Hera’s son, whose handiwork surpasses that of the other heavenly gods.

cards.label: Zeus
cards.general: The ruler of the gods, whose weapon is the thunderbolt.
cards.here: He swallows Metis and later gives birth to Athena from his head.

cards.label: Cronus
cards.general: Zeus’s father, who ruled the gods before him.
cards.here: The poem calls Zeus “son of Cronus.”

cards.label: Oceanus and Tethys
cards.general: Ancient water deities, parents of rivers and many goddesses.
cards.here: Their daughter is the woman Zeus sleeps with, apparently Metis.

cards.label: Metis
cards.general: A goddess of intelligence and cunning.
cards.here: Athena’s mother, who remains inside Zeus after he swallows her.

cards.label: Pallas Athena
cards.general: A goddess of wisdom, crafts, and warfare. Pallas is another name used for her.
cards.here: She is born from Zeus’s head wearing battle gear.

cards.label: Triton
cards.general: The name of a river whose location is uncertain.
cards.here: Athena’s birth takes place beside its banks.

cards.label: Olympus
cards.general: The mountain where the gods have their homes.
cards.here: The poem compares the goddess’s skill with that of all the gods living there.

cards.label: Aegis
cards.general: A divine protective covering, often pictured as a shield or cloak.
cards.here: The bracketed line describes it as Athena’s armor, terrifying enough to scatter armies.

uncertainties: These supplementary verses are translated as a separate textual variant, not incorporated into the main numbered text.
The source has a gap after 929f. Its extent and missing words are unknown; no connecting words have been supplied.
The daughter of Oceanus and Tethys in 929e–f is apparently Metis, but the gap interrupts the connection.

The wording and connections in 929q–r are obscure. “Had found a place” interprets παρέδεκτο as “had been received” inside Zeus, with Metis as the goddess. The connection expressed by “from there” is also uncertain.

Line 929s is marked as deleted in the supplied text. It is included in square brackets as requested. “She” is taken to mean Metis; the following line is understood to describe Zeus bringing Athena to birth with the aegis.
